source.title: Analysis of Bootstrap and Subsampling in High-dimensional Regularized Regression
source.authors: Lucas Clart'e; Adrien Vandenbroucque; Guillaume Dalle; Bruno Loureiro; Florent Krzakala; L. Zdeborová

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses double-descent-like behavior, but its reported results concern estimator bias and variance for high-dimensional regression and resampling, not the test-error curves or other measures named by the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The text reports local maxima in true and resampled bias and variance near d=n for low-regularization ridge and logistic regression. These are not test-error results. The paper also gives an equation relating prediction variance to test error, but does not report a test-error sweep; cited results about neural-network and random-feature double descent are not this study’s results.
record.test_reason: The paper's results are asymptotic and simulated bias and variance of ridge and logistic estimators, plus their resampling estimates, as n/d varies. The true squared bias plus variance equals the estimator MSE, which for ridge is test error minus noise (Appendix D). But the paper never reports that sum or any test-error sweep. It reports bias and variance separately, as uncertainty-quantification targets, and calls their local maxima near d=n only 'reminiscent' of double descent. No version's measure (test error or risk against size, epochs or samples) is reported. The finding belongs under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. Resampling methods show double-descent-like behavior in high dimensions and give consistent error estimates only at large α. For α<1 their predictions are inconsistent even with optimal regularization.
record.recipe_differences: The paper analyzes regularized generalized linear regression and resampling asymptotically; it does not perform the deep-network size, epoch, or data sweeps of the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that regularization mitigates the double-descent-like behavior; it compares λ=10^-2 with λ=1 in its regression analyses.

fits_no_version.finding: At λ=10^-2, true and resampled (bootstrap, subsampling, jackknife) estimator bias and variance show a local maximum near d=n for ridge and logistic regression. At λ=1 (optimal for ridge) the pattern is mitigated.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In high-dimensional GLMs, estimator bias and variance, and their resampling estimates, peak near n=d at weak regularization; stronger regularization suppresses the peak.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence, 2024
record.problems: The reported double-descent-like finding concerns bias and variance, not the test-error curves in the claim. Numerical comparisons use d=200 and B=10 resamples; the relevant local-maximum description is qualitative.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows: plots report multiple resampling-method curves, but the text’s local-maximum statement does not attribute that qualitative result separately to each method. Numerical figure values were not extracted as test-error findings.

untested.parts: Model-size sweep in deep networks; no networks studied.
Test error over training epochs; not studied.
Test error as sample count rises near the threshold. Only bias and variance components against n/d are shown, never their sum or the test error.
Risk past interpolation across model classes; test risk of ridge or logistic against n/d is not reported.
Effective-complexity prediction of peak location; not studied.
Noise dependence, multiple peaks, and disappearance under optimal regularization of the test-error peak. The paper only says regularization mitigates the bias and variance maxima.
Effective parameter count turning the second descent into a U-curve; not studied.

record.verdict_notes: Borderline case. Appendix D shows that for ridge the estimator MSE (bias² + variance) equals test error minus noise, so the plotted components bear indirectly on a sample-wise (V3-like) peak in linear models. However, the paper reports neither the summed test error nor numbers at the peak; the statement is qualitative (Section 5.2). If a curator decides component-level peaks count, V3 and V6 would be the candidate versions, in ridge regression at λ=10^-2 versus λ=1. The double-descent results the paper cites for random features and neural networks are not its own results.

versions.untested_parts: Model-size test-error curve in deep networks and its peak near the training-set interpolation size.
Effect of increasing training sample count near the interpolation threshold on test error.
Risk curves across model classes as capacity passes the interpolation point.
Whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak location across size, epochs, and sample count.
Whether test-error peaks depend on label noise or variance, split into multiple peaks, or disappear under optimally tuned regularization.
Whether an effective parameter count turns second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: ridge regression
rows.operation_detail: Analyzed bias and variance as the sample-to-dimension ratio α=n/d varies.
rows.note: The text reports this pattern for the true and resampled bias; the statement does not enumerate individual resampling methods.
rows.check: Condition 'ratio: local maximum around d=n' restates the result rather than a condition; the sweep variable is α=n/d. The pattern is stated in text for λ=10^-2 only, and the λ=1 panels are the contrast. State 'observed' refers to the study's own measure, not a claim version.
